claims.text: W particles should be coated with a thin vapor-deposited Ni interlayer before consolidation with Cu by spark plasma sintering.
The Ni coating will form a graded interfacial layer between W and Cu.
Ni reacts or interacts with both W and Cu at the interface.
The Ni interlayer improves wetting between W and Cu.
The Ni interlayer reduces the surface-energy mismatch between W and Cu.
The Ni interlayer facilitates diffusion bonding between W and Cu.
Improved wetting and interfacial bonding will reduce void formation during consolidation.
Improved wetting and interfacial bonding will limit phase separation during consolidation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have a lower void volume fraction than composites fabricated without a Ni interlayer.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have a more homogeneous microstructure than the baseline.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than the baseline.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have better mechanical durability under irradiation than the baseline.
Vapor-coated W powders followed by spark plasma sintering typically produce phase separation, voids, and compromised thermal transport.
Phase separation and voids in W–Cu composites impair thermal transport and mechanical durability.
The intervention can remain effective under fusion-reactor thermal loads and irradiation.
An excessively thick Ni coating may reduce the intervention's effectiveness.
Processing temperatures that fail to preserve the Ni-mediated interfacial structure may reduce effectiveness.
The long-term irradiation stability of the Ni-mediated W–Cu interface is not yet quantified.

contradictions.description: The named baseline is described as vapor-coated W powder followed by SPS, but the predicted-outcome language calls it a composite without Ni and the experiment uses entirely uncoated W particles. These are not necessarily the same fabrication baseline, so the comparator is internally inconsistent.
